newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crudes-LLS tightens up as July bbls eyed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crudes-LLS tightens up as July bbls eyed.

text.p: U.S. cash crude price differentials were mostly steady early Monday as outright prices firmed with futures, though Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James (LLS) edged up a few cents in line with North Sea Brent, market players said.

Traders said that U.S. refineries are starting to look for July barrels in earnest this week, but they noted that the relatively firm price for marker West Texas Intermediate/Cushing doesn't reflect the ample crude supply situation, market participants said.

In early trading on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) was up around 15 cents at $21.03 a barrel. And with exchange-for-physical (EFP) premiums at between 10-15 cents, cash WTI was about 13-18 cents above Friday's late levels.
There were no trades in dometic grades seen early on, though LLS was quoted at a 13/15 cents discount to WTI, about 3/5 cents up on Friday.

The firmer LLS market was a function of a slight improvement in prompt Brent, with which it competes, traders said. Brent had slumped by 50 cents last week to trade at a discount of 30 cents to July Brent, but it was being quoted at firmer levels Monday, they said.
Other grades were hardly changed from Friday, with West Texas Sour/Midland bid at $1.60 under WTI, Eugene Island offered at a $1.55 discount and WTI/Midland at a 37/34 cents discount.

Though WTI was being propped up by a combination of shorts on the futures market and the firm EFP premium as the market anticipates another heavy foreign crude delivery against the July future, the market fundamentals point to easier cash prices, traders said.

"Storage is full and even with near 100 percent (refinery) runs last week we had a rise in crude stocks," said one trader, referring to the American Petroleum Institute report for the week ended May 23.

That report showed stocks up nearly 1.4 million barrels on the week and running more than 18 million barrels ahead of the same week a year earlier even with refinery runs at nearly 97 percent nationwide.
Traders have also noted that the relatively firm refinery margins in the U.S. have lured more foreign barrels from Europe and even Asia.
